# …and about 30 more fields

And the controls?

  • Can it be merged now? By which methods? With what fields?
  • Can I comment? Reopen? Request a review?
  • Answered elsewhere: docs pages, an SDK, a 13.5 MB OpenAPI file, read by a developer and coded into a client.

The same gap as AWS’s three docs pages, in the preview.
say: Start where most APIs are. GitHub's pull request, as data only, shortened from about 40 fields. It says what the pull request is. It says nothing about what you can do with it. Those controls live out of band: docs pages, an SDK, a 13.5 MB OpenAPI file. Like AWS's three docs pages in the preview.

deck:ref.name: rule-3
deck:ref.label: Rule 3 · Describe the media type
deck:ref.title: Spend the effort on media types
deck:ref.summary: In brief: describe media types and relations, not which methods go to which URIs. This is what HEART's spec is.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should spend almost all of its descriptive effort in defining the media type(s) used for representing resources and driving application state, or in defining extended relation names and/or hypertext-enabled mark-up for existing standard media types. Any effort spent describing what methods to use on what URIs of interest should be entirely defined within the scope of the processing rules for a media type (and, in most cases, already defined by existing media types). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-6
deck:ref.label: Rule 6 · The bookmark
deck:ref.title: Enter with a bookmark; follow what's offered
deck:ref.summary: In brief: one URI and known media types to start; every next step chosen from what the server put in the answer.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should be entered with no prior knowledge beyond the initial URI (bookmark) and set of standardized media types that are appropriate for the intended audience (i.e., expected to be understood by any client that might use the API). From that point on, all application state transitions must be driven by client selection of server-provided choices that are present in the received representations or implied by the user’s manipulation of those representations. The transitions may be determined (or limited by) the client’s knowledge of media types and resource communication mechanisms, both of which may be improved on-the-fly (e.g., code-on-demand). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”
